front.title: Uniform Resource Identifiers for Television Broadcasts

section.name: Introduction
section.t: World-Wide Web browsers are starting to appear on a variety of consumer electronic devices, such as television sets and television set-top boxes, which are capable of receiving television programming from either terrestrial broadcast, satellite broadcast, or cable. In this context there is a need to reference television broadcasts using the URI format described in . This document describes a widely-implemented URI scheme to refer to such broadcasts.

section.name: Television URI
section.t: The basic structure of a television URI is:
where broadcast is a description of the data source. The description takes the form of a DNS-style identifier for a particular broadcaster or television network. For example:
section.artwork: tv:wqed.org the WQED station tv:nbc.com the NBC network

section.name: Scheme-only form
section.t: A simplest form of the "tv:" URI scheme is used to refer to the "current" or "default" channel:

This URI refers to whichever television broadcast is currently being received by the device. It is often used in combination with HTML content that is actually being broadcast along with the audio and video, where the meaning of "current broadcast" is quite unambiguous (because it is the broadcast along with which the content containing the URI was received). This is in fact the most common usage of the "tv:" scheme today, and is explicitly referenced by the recently published specification of the Advanced Television Enhancement Forum .

section.name: DNS-style identifiers
section.t: Television broadcasts traditionally have been identified in a variety of ways. All terrestrial television broadcasters are assigned call signs (such as "KDKA" or "WQED") to identify their signal. These are generally assigned by national authorities (such as the Federal Communications Commission in the United States) and are world unique. The global namespace is managed by the International Telecommunications Union, which assigns portions to member countries (see ).

Many modern television networks are not broadcasted over-the-air, but available only through cable or satellite subscriptions. The identifiers for these networks (such as the familiar "CNN" and "HBO") are not regulated at this time. In some countries, even over-the-air broadcasters use these sorts of identifiers, rather than call signs.

Unfortunately, these two namespaces overlap, with most network identifiers also being valid call signs. Furthermore, network identifiers are not world unique, and many cases exist of name collisions. (For example, both the Australian Broadcast Corporation and the American Broadcasting Company identify themselves as "ABC".) In order to ensure uniqueness, the "tv:" scheme uses DNS-style identifiers for all broadcast streams. Because these build on the existing registration system for DNS hostname, all name collisions can be resolved through the existing DNS dispute resolution processes.
In the simplest form, domain names themselves are used as broadcast identifiers. For example:
section.artwork: tv:abc.com the American Broadcast Company tv:abc.co.au the Australian Broadcast Corporation
section.t: In some cases, networks have multiple broadcast streams that need to be distinguished. This is also handled in DNS style:
section.artwork: tv:east.hbo.com HBO East tv:west.hbo.com HBO West
section.t: It is important to note that these DNS-style identifiers need not match real hostnames; they should not be resolved to IP addresses using DNS. Thus, using the terms as defined in RFC 2396, the "tv:" scheme is a Uniform Resource Identifier and not a Uniform Resource Locator.

In order to support these identifiers in a "tv:" URI, a receiver must implement a means to map known identifiers to frequencies. The nature of this map and the way in which it is used are currently browser- and device-specific and are beyond the scope of this document. In this way, the "tv:" scheme is somewhat analogous to the "news:" and "file:" schemes in [1]: it merely names a television broadcast signal but assumes that the local browser has some means for actually retrieving that signal on the local device. A variety of software systems currently provide device-specific mappings from such identifiers to specific channel numbers or directly to frequencies. These systems can be incorporated into television sets or set-top boxes to facilitate the interpretation of television URIs by the client device.

section.name: Obsolete forms
section.t: Previous drafts of this specification allowed broadcasts to be identified by channel numbers, such as "tv:4", and this form is currently supported by several independent platforms. The channel numbers generally correspond to tuning frequencies in the various national broadcast frequency standards; for example, "tv:4" in the United states would be found at 66 MHz. However, because this mapping of channel numbers to frequencies varies from country to country, this form is particularly ill-suited to use on the Internet.

Previous drafts also allowed network identifiers and call signs to be used directly as broadcast identifiers, as in "tv:abc" and "tv:kron". These forms should not be used because of the name collision issues described in the previous section.

section.name: BNF for Television URIs
section.t: The following is a formal specification for the new URIs:
section.artwork: tvuri = "tv:" [ broadcast ] broadcast = dns-identifier dns-identifier = *( domainlabel "." ) toplabel [ "." ] domainlabel = alphanum | alphanum *( alphanum | "-" ) alphanum toplabel = alpha | alpha *( alphanum | "-" ) alphanum
section.t: The definitions of alpha and alphanum are from . Furthermore, the definition of dns-identifier is identical to the definition of hostname in RFC 2396, and is case-insensitive.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This new URI scheme is subject to the same security implications as the general URI scheme described in . It is possible that the mere act of viewing a television broadcast signal may cause costs to be incurred to the viewer in some instances (e.g., "pay-per-view" movies and events). Any software that uses this URI scheme to allow automatic tuning of a client device to a particular television broadcast signal should alert users before performing actions that may incur costs to the user.
